title: the dice game
hook: Duryodhana walks through Maya's hall, mistakes floor for water and water for floor, and hears laughter

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shishupala's light rose and entered Krishna, and the Rajasuya was finished. Your line was where you'd rather turn that light. Did you notice where your attention went? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

The guests have gone home. But one guest has stayed behind. Duryodhana lingers at Indraprastha with his uncle Shakuni, wandering through the great hall the asura builder Maya made for the Pandavas. It's a hall of wonders, and wonders can be tricky. Floors that look like water. Water that looks like floor. Doors that seem open and aren't. A new story starts here, and it's called the dice game. But it doesn't start with dice. It starts with a man walking through a beautiful room and getting it wrong, again and again.
screen: `ONE GUEST STAYS BEHIND.` → `MAYA'S HALL OF WONDERS.` → `IT STARTS WITHOUT DICE.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Duryodhana comes to a spot on the floor that looks like a pool. It's crystal, but he takes it for water, and he gathers up his clothes to wade across. Nothing wet. Then he comes to a real pool, so clear it looks like solid floor, and he walks straight in, clothes and all. And here's the line that hurts: Bhima sees it, and laughs. The servants laugh too. Yudhishthira, the host, sends him dry clothes. It doesn't help. A little further on, Duryodhana tries to walk through a doorway that looks open, and strikes his head on a wall of crystal. At another door, which really is open, he holds back, thinking it closed. By the end of his visit, the hall has fooled him over and over, and his mistakes have had an audience. Hold onto what happened here, because it's small, and it's going to be enormous. Nobody attacked Duryodhana. Nobody planned this. A beautiful building and a little laughter. But he has just watched kings from near and far bring gifts to his cousin, and now his cousin's house has made him look like a fool. The poem is careful here. It doesn't excuse him for what comes next. It just shows us the moment the wound opens. The dice game, when it comes, will look like a game of chance. But its roots are here, in a man walking alone through a room that made him feel small, with laughter behind him.
screen: `CRYSTAL TAKEN FOR WATER.` · `A POOL TAKEN FOR FLOOR.` · `BHIMA LAUGHS.` · `A DOOR THAT ISN'T THERE.` · then, large: `THE WOUND OPENS BEFORE THE DICE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes close, or lower them to the floor. Bring to mind a moment you laughed at someone's mistake, even kindly, even a little. A wrong turn, a spill, a slip of the tongue. Now see it from their side for a moment: the heat in the face, the wish to disappear. You don't need to feel guilty. Just let both views sit side by side, theirs and yours. If you pray, you can remember them kindly in your prayer. If not, simply wish them ease. The bell holds the time.
Dyuta, the game of dice this story is named for. A story that doesn't begin with dice, but with Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at as he falls.
Your line: help before you laugh. Today, when someone slips up in front of you, help before you laugh. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Some Hindu storytellers treat Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall as the opening of the dice-game story, the small wound that leads to the great quarrel.

myth: the dice game story begins with dice
it begins with Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall and laughed at.
Duryodhana walked into a real pool he took for floor
the water was so clear it looked solid, and he fell in.
Bhima and the servants laughed; Yudhishthira sent him dry clothes.

fork.setup: you're Bhima. your cousin, who has never wished you well, has just walked into a pool in full royal dress. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Bhima laughs, and the servants with him. it's a small moment that the poem lets grow very large.

original.note: Sanskrit dyūta: dice play, gambling; the name of the section of the poem this story begins.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dice game is about luck.
what it means: it grows from Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall, after watching the kings honor his cousin.
what a scholar hears: the poem opens the dice story with a scene of mistaken appearances, and the game itself will turn on things not being what they seem.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana in Maya's hall: crystal taken for water, the pool, Bhima's laughter, the doors)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the sequence in Ganguli: crystal mistaken for water, the clear pool he falls into, Bhima and the servants laughing, Yudhishthira sending clothes, the closed and open doors.

Popular retellings add Draupadi laughing and a taunt about the blind king's son; this script leaves that out. A Keeper should check what Ganguli's text says about who laughed before any later day mentions Draupadi here.
The original note says Dyuta is the name of the section; confirm (Ganguli titles it Dyuta Parva).
The trapdoor's third floor is an interpretive reading of theme, not a textual claim; a Keeper may prefer a plainer line.
howItsDone 'often treat' is a general claim; soften if needed.
